title: Diwali on a Plate: Mithai, Namkeen and the Thali at the Centre
excerpt: From gulab jamun and kaju katli to samosas, chivda and a shared vegetarian thali, two guides map the sweets, snacks and mains that define a Diwali table.
body:
• Diwali food centres on mithai — sweets such as gulab jamun, jalebi, barfi, kaju katli and ladoo — exchanged in boxes and served to guests, according to Food Network UK.
  • Savoury namkeen balances the sweets: samosas, pakora, chivda and murukku are the snacks both sources return to.
  • There is no single traditional Diwali menu, Food Network UK notes; many households serve a vegetarian thali of paneer curries, dals, chickpeas, pulao or biryani and breads.
  • In 2026 Diwali falls on Sunday, November 8, with the five-day celebration running from Dhanteras on November 6, according to the Rohan's Indian Bistro guide.

Diwali is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains and by more than a billion people all over the world, Food Network UK notes, usually over five or six days between the middle of October and the middle of November. Food is firmly at the heart of it — from syrup-soaked sweets to savoury snacks and lavish feasts shared with whoever walks in.

A second guide, from Rohan's Indian Bistro, puts it in household terms: a table that is never empty, with sweets passed between neighbours and snacks refilled all evening. In 2026 Diwali falls on Sunday, November 8, with the five-day celebration running from Dhanteras on November 6.

Mithai: The Sweets That Get Gifted

It is not a proper Diwali celebration without mithai, from the ancient Sanskrit word mishta, meaning sweet or sugary, Food Network UK explains. Boxes of colourful treats are exchanged with relatives, friends and neighbours, while homemade favourites are served to guests with tea or after a grand feast.

Ladoo come in many varieties. Motichoor ladoo are made from tiny fried droplets of chickpea flour (besan) batter soaked in sugar syrup, while besan ladoo are made from roasted chickpea flour, ghee, sugar, and sometimes fruit, nuts or cardamom. Barfi, a rich, fudge-like sweet traditionally made with khoya (reduced milk solids) and sugar, comes in flavours from coconut and pistachio to mango, chocolate, rosewater and saffron, and is usually cut into squares or diamonds and decorated with edible silver foil called vark.

Gulab jamun are soft, deep-fried dough balls made from khoya often mixed with a little flour — some modern recipes use milk powder instead — soaked in warm sugar syrup scented with cardamom, saffron or rosewater. Jalebi are spiral-shaped, deep-fried sweets of fermented flour batter soaked in warm sugar syrup flavoured with saffron, rosewater, cardamom or lemon juice, crispy on the outside and chewy on the inside. Kaju katli, made from finely ground cashews and sugar and sometimes ghee, is cut into thin diamond shapes and sometimes topped with edible silver leaf.

Food Network UK also lists rasgulla from Bengal and Odisha — chhena balls in light syrup — and soan papdi, a flaky gram-flour sweet flavoured with cardamom.

Namkeen: The Savoury Balance

Alongside mithai, Diwali tables are filled with namkeen, the salty, spicy and crunchy snacks, Food Network UK notes. Fried or roasted snacks made with lentils, chickpea flour, rice flour, nuts and spices are especially common.

Samosas are crisp, triangular pastries stuffed most often with potato, onion and peas, deep-fried until golden and served hot with chutneys; some varieties are filled with lentils, minced meat or paneer. Chivda is a crunchy mix traditionally made with flattened rice, peanuts, cashews, almonds, roasted chickpeas and fried lentils, flavoured with curry leaves, green chillies, mustard seeds and turmeric. Pakora are bite-sized fritters made by coating vegetables, paneer, or sometimes chicken, in a seasoned chickpea-flour batter before deep-frying. Murukku are crispy twisted snacks made from rice flour and urad dal flour, often flavoured with cumin, sesame seeds or chilli and shaped through a press before frying.

The Rohan's guide lists a similar savoury set — samosas, pakoras, chakli (spiral-shaped crisp snacks) and namak pare — typically served with chai and passed around all evening.

The Main Meal: A Thali, Not a Fixed Menu

Generally speaking, Diwali does not have what would be called a traditional menu, Food Network UK says. For many, the main meal is vegetarian and often built around a generous selection of dishes served on a single platter, known as a thali, made for sharing. A celebratory spread might include rich paneer curries, slow-cooked dals, chickpeas, fragrant pulao or biryani, and breads such as naan, roti or puffed poori,.

The Rohan's guide agrees that the main meal varies by family: many households cook vegetarian during the festival, though practices differ, and a typical spread might include paneer dishes in rich gravies, dal makhani, chickpea curries, pulao or biryani, naan or puri, raita and pickles. Masala chai and lassi accompany the sweets, it adds.

For diaspora readers abroad, both guides point to the same formula: mithai to gift, namkeen for guests, and a shared thali-style main.
